Frankly, the weighting for the final was slightly absurd, and even though the weightings are understandable given how Homework is weighted 10% often now in the MATH department, it's still rather annoying.

There was a great deal of anxiety based on prior reviews about the final, given that Stefan's tests are generally quite easy, but overall, I thought the final was rather fair difficulty-wise, and not too much more difficult than his midterms (85% median for finals versus 90-95% medians for the midterm). The non-final tests are honestly rather easy, which is a relief.

I unfortunately found the class... a bit disorganized overall though. One of the TA's for the course often gave information that turned out not to be true, and there always seemed to be a disconnect between the TA and Stefan's way of teaching, which could make things confusing when going into a discussion. One of the tests had an issue with a question on a topic that was not tested on, though luckily, this issue was resolved. I also often found the way Stefan thought to be a bit handwavy overall. This might be a bit of bias due to taking prior math classes, and partly because it is a 200-level class, but Stefan gives very brief and vague explanations of some topics. Even though they aren't often tested on, they can come off a bit strange. Stefan also does not record, though his notes are rather helpful.

Really, though, most of these points are nitpicks, and Stefan is all in all a pretty great teacher.

Great lecturer, made topics easy to understand, exams were pretty easy (exam averages were B+/A- for all three midterms). No required work in discussion sections. There are 4 Matlab projects but the lowest score is dropped making it essentially 3 Matlab projects. Matlab projects are auto-graded instead of manually graded which I preferred but this did lead to a few frustrating moments with the autograder not working as expected (nothing that couldn't be sorted out by emailing Stefan ofc). Overall I'd recommend!

She doesn’t do a very good job with lectures. They are kind of hard to understand and over complicates some stuff. She does have lecture summaries that are helpful if you miss class or something. Her tests are very easy and she does care a lot about her students, but her tests are so easy that when it comes to the final that she doesn’t write, you are very unprepared. The class average for tests were significantly lower than the final, around 15% lower. If you take her, don’t take her tests as a baseline for how the final will be.

I think Dr. Doucette was a great teacher and is going to be even better when you take her because of her constant goal to receive our feedback and improve. Admittedly, at the start of the semester her lectures were a bit rough because she was using the chalkboard in a classroom where it was hard to see, and she was kinda all over the place and explained certain concepts too much before doing examples. She overcomplicated a lot of things. However, she consistently asked for our feedback, so she switched to a projector, started doing more examples, and she became more confident in how she explained things, and I ended up finding her lectures super helpful. All I had to do was examples from the textbook to study after getting the basis of each topic down from her lectures. 

She gives weekly discussion quizzes but they're free because she sends an announcement and describes the exact type of question she's gonna ask on it, so as long as you do practice problems to study beforehand you'll do fine. She also dropped 2 quizzes. I found these helpful for keeping up with the content, as every quiz was basically just one exam-type problem, so by the time the exam comes you've already done each type of question.

Her exams were super fair for the most part; the first exam was exactly like the practice exam she had given us and the third exam was easier than the practice exam she gave us. The only exception was exam 2, which was honestly a lot harder than I expected but I still did good (almost every niche thing you'd assume she wouldn't include on it, she did, like the dirac delta and heaviside functions for laplace and also a pretty hard version of undetermined coefficients). Her exam averages were 90.2, 76.4, and 84.9 for exams 1, 2, and 3 respectively. 

Overall she's a sweetheart and I highly recommend!!

HE IS NOT A GOOD PROFESSOR! His mumbles during his lectures, makes many mistakes, and goes way too fast. The first midterm was unnecessarily difficult (class avg of 52%) and only 2 problems (each with part a and b). it's kind of crazy because each midterm is 200 points (20% of the entire grade) He does give a retake opportunity for each midterm, but they aren't much easier. The second midterm was much better (class avg 76). The class is curved such that an 85% is an A (A- if right on the border), 75% is a B and so on. There are 4 MATLAB projects which are very easy and in class quizzes that are directly from the suggested problems almost every week usually 10pts each (Midterms are 200, Final is 400). Otherwise, there isn't any homework. The textbook that he uses is mid, Paul's Online Math Notes was a much more useful resource. Attendance isn't mandatory but you risk missing an in-class quiz as he usually doesn't announce them.
Exams are fair and u get a lot of partial credit. She's also nice and her lectures got better throughout the semester.

Stefan as a Lecturer is great and just sitting in lecture can give you a pretty complete grasp of the material. He writes through problems on paper and will generally spare the class from needing to do tedious algebra on a problem when he is teaching a higher-level solution process. This as well the MATLAB assignments are mostly straightforward and the class offers a lot of support for them. Where the class is difficult is in the grading breakdown, as there is a 50% final which can be truly make or break at the end of the semester and can singlehandedly tank your grade if youre not careful, so just beware and try to do best on the midterms so you can stomach a loss if it does happen.

Seems like a chill person, though stopped going after week 2 since lectures were just reading off of Justin's notes. Class is not too hard, especially if you've had prior experience with Lin Alg. Matlab assignments were a decent grade booster and didn't even show up on the exam. Midterms were reasonable, the TAs taught everything in the lectures in 1/10th of the time in weekly discussion sections.

I always sat in the front, paid attention, asked questions, and really enjoyed her lectures. I actually disagree with people saying that her lectures are disorganized. Her lectures always have the same structure: Setup / Motivation -> Theory -> Example. Not to mention, examples are mixed in with theory so that people follow what is going on. I found her lectures very well structured.

On top of amazing lectures, her class is also super organized. The class ELMS page is the most organized class I have ever had. She provides MANY different resources for students, and on top of that her own notes, which I found very very useful. For all exams she gives practice exams, and the discussions are also amazing and amazing practice for exams. She is also a very nice person, and genuinely willing to help. It is clear that she genuinely cares about her students.

Overall, I could not have hoped for a better experience with this class. If you really want to learn Diff Eq and understand it then she is the way to go without a doubt.

Nice guy and all, I know many students did very well, but I kind of ended this course with the same level of knowledge I started with. Everything was just kind of use this formula get this answer, but maybe that's just the nature of diff eq. Justin's notes carried me on their back sometimes using linear algebra was much easier then the in class method.

Very nice person, exams were fair, and I didn't have to dedicate much time to studying in this class (though I did come in with a strong foundation from previous math classes). She is very understanding about extenuating circumstances in life, hence why she decided to drop two quizzes instead of only one. I would definitely recommend this professor. She provided a lot of practice material, and the practice exams especially were very useful. I would recommend this professor to anyone.

Great professor. Is a lot younger than most profs at umd which definitely helped. Great lecturer, and while he followed Levermore's notes for a good bit of the class, you could tell the aspects of the lecture that he worked on to make it easier to understand. The class had a good bit of theory, but nothing that is too hard to understand with the notes. Would take for another class.

I took this professor at community college for a winter semester and omg her teaching style is the worst i've ever seen. Her teaching consisted of fill in the blanks worksheets that made no sense. We are not highschoolers or middle schoolers to use this type of teaching format. If you want to pass MATH246 do not take this professor!!
Worst professor I have ever had, lectures are not helpful. He cannot go through an example without making multiple mistakes. Really should not be a professor at all.

By far the worst teacher I have ever had, and hopefully will ever have in my life. I had no idea that teachers could get this bad, and I have had some very bad teachers. To all those interested in taking any of his courses, please read this review in its entirety. There is much to discuss. 

His lecture style is flying through practice problems and complex concepts as such speed that no one in the class takes notes, because they can't. His lectures are also riddled with errors such that going into lectures with an understanding of the material will leave you with less understanding than what you arrived with. He also rarely posts his slides "to not to compete with the book". Thus, the only way to learn is through the book and scattered online resources, and attending the lectures is a waste of time that you must do because there is a chance of a quiz, which will occur at an unnanounced day every week. If that was all, I would have probably given him 3-4 stars, but alas it gets worse.

At the beginning of the semester, he gives out a syllabus that states that every quiz will be based on certain problems from the textbook, that you should do as homework. As you will find out if you take him, that is rarely the case, and the quiz averages will hover near 50%, escalating to a max of 80% for supposedly "easy quizzes". They are not curved.

To further the discussion of quizzes, this semester he decided to give out a quiz the day before spring break. He sent an email thereafter containing only the words "attached are notes from class" with a pdf. As students had gotten used to his notes being mostly useless, those who had to miss due to travel/seeing family stuck to reading the book. Attached at the bottom of 26 pages of notes was a 20 point quiz (double the score of all other quizzes) which was to be turned in in class the day after spring break. Those who never saw the quiz were told that he "did all he could do" and they could not take the quiz - they should have known it was attached in an email that had it hidden, with no mention of it in the actual email or any announcement. Thus, university approved absences were nullified.

To delve further into the frustration in the difficulty of scoring high in a supposedly grade-boosting portion of the course would not bode well in the interest of time. However the above example should be taken as just that, with the expectation that similar events will occur with relatively high frequency. 

Since the majority of students struggle with his tests, he issues a makeup for each one. However his makeups are significantly harder than the first ones, and so the average for these is 30 points worse than that of the first one. The tests are uncurved, and if you take the makeup and turn it in it replaces your first score even if it is lower. You may be thinking that this is a very harsh policy, since the tests are already so difficult. You are correct.

For our last midterm, he explicitly told us that a certain topic would be on the exam, and it wasn't. In its place was a topic that students didn't study because he stated that "the new material would be represented by a tank mixing problem". Of course, this meant that many students didn't know how to do a quarter of his exam, because there are only 4 questions. Although this is not normal, the tests are hard enough regardless. There are 2 questions each with 2 parts, each 50 points. He also commonly gives students 0 out of 50 for problems that were done slightly wrong, or gives students much less than they should. Sometimes this is fixed with a regrade. Sometimes not. To truly break the camel's back, his exams are only 40 minutes long in a 50 minute lecture period. 

Now for some miscellaneous points. There are no discussions, which would probably help a lot given the difficulty. Only real homeworks are the matlabs, which are very complex given that the course has 0 coding prerequisites - there is a textbook you must buy to even understand what to do on them. These are supposed to be the real grade boosters - hovering at an average of about 70-80%. Over half of his students currently have failing grades in this course, even accounting for his "curve". Still interested in learning differential equations? 

I digress to the positives:
The final becomes a collective exam score (replacing midterms) if you do better on it than the midterms, but good luck if you think you'll be able to use that.
The class is curved such that 680/800 total points is an A, 600/800 is a B, and so on. However as stated above, this is pretty negligable.
He seems like a pretty cool person. I almost feel bad leaving this review, and then I remember what his teaching has put me through.

Big Stefan, my goat. Genuinely nice guy and great professor.

IGNORE MY GRADE, this was the last math class I have to take so I had math-senioritis. I genuinely like Stefan.

His lectures are great, he goes through examples in class. Very responsive to questions. My only complaint is that I didn't really retain much info from the course itself after the semester ended (but I might just be a bad student lol).

Yes diff eq is hard, and you will have to study a lot. However, there are a ton of online resources for practice on the UMD math archive page.

name: MATH246
title: Differential Equations for Scientists and Engineers
description: Prerequisite: Minimum grade of C- in MATH141. Credit only granted for: MATH246 or MATH341. An introduction to the basic methods of solving ordinary differential equations. Equations of first and second order, linear differential equations, Laplace transforms, numerical methods and the qualitative theory of differential equations. All sections will use MATLAB.
